data_section_full_text:
3. Data
We obtained actual and forecast annual earnings per share (EPS) values for the
years 1986 to 1996 from the Zacks Investment Research data base. This data base
includes both forecast and actual EPS values in conformance with Zacks’ definition
of earnings per share from continuing operations before extraordinary, nonrecurring,
and special items. To obtain annual earnings estimates and realizations, we multiply Zacks EPS values by COMPUSTAT annual item #54 (common shares used to
calculate EPS) and COMPUSTAT annual item #27 (a factor to adjust annual item
54 for stock splits and stock dividends). To ensure comparability of forecast and
“actual” earnings, all comparisons are based on the forecast and actual numbers
reported by Zacks. <sup>9</sup>

Since our data comprise a broad range of firm sizes, we scale all earnings
values. A variety of approaches to scaling have been used in the accounting and
finance literature, including scaling by market value, book value, sales, total assets,
and number of shares. Results are reported here for variables scaled by market
value, as in BD. The level of earnings for year t is scaled by beginning-of-year
market value of common equity for year t (that is, the market value at the end of


CAR Vol. 20 No. 2 (Summer 2003)

262 Contemporary Accounting Research


year t - 1), computed as common shares outstanding (COMPUSTAT annual item
25) × price per share at fiscal year-end (COMPUSTAT annual item #199), both as
of the end of year t - 1. Similarly, the change in earnings between years t - 1 and t
is scaled by the market value of equity at the end of year t - 2.

The analysis of forecast errors is restricted to forecasts of annual earnings
available on the Zacks database that meet the following requirements:


1. earnings announcement date is available on COMPUSTAT industrial or research
quarterly files and prior-year market value is available on COMPUSTAT industrial or research annual files;

2. firms are neither financial (SIC codes 4400 to 5000) nor utilities (SIC codes
6000 to 6500);

3. forecast release date is within 360 days of the COMPUSTAT earnings
announcement date;

4. earnings announcement date is not more than 150 days after fiscal year-end;
and

5. actual earnings is available on the Zacks data base.


Financial and utility firms are excluded from the analysis by requirement (2), consistent with the decision in BD to eliminate firms that are subject to more complex
earnings-management incentives due to regulation or other factors. Requirement
(4) is intended to eliminate those few firms that report unusually late, because our
classification of the timing of forecasts relative to the announcement date makes
interpretation of these cases difficult. Taken together, the data availability requirements undoubtedly lead to a sample containing larger, more well-established firms
than the overall population of firms.

Table 1 presents the number of Zacks reported forecasts meeting selection criteria by year, along with the numbers of forecasts, firms, and analysts. The number
of individual forecasts, the number of firms for which forecasts are available, and
the number of analysts all increase substantially between 1986 and 1996 as the
Zacks data base expands. The increases across time are fairly smooth, except for
1995, when Zacks’ forecast disclosure policies were amended and therefore
reduced the availability of forecasts. Table 1 summarizes our starting data set,
though many of our tests employ restricted subsets of this data. The number of
firm-year observations contributing to each test is noted in our tables of results.

Each annual earnings forecast record in the Zacks data base represents either
an analyst’s first estimate of earnings for a fiscal year, a change in the analyst’s
estimate (from a previously reported estimate), or an unchanged analyst’s estimate
when the previous estimate is more than 120 days old. <sup>10</sup> For each firm and fiscal
year, the Zacks data base includes forecasts released at various dates by a number
of analysts.

There are many alternative ways to define firm-year forecasts, including both
individual analyst forecasts and composite forecasts. O’Brien (1988) shows that

recent 30 days is more accurate than the most recent forecast for large firms,
though less accurate for small firms. Richardson, Teoh, and Wysocki (1999) provide evidence that forecast bias moves from optimism toward pessimism during
